reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard rheumatology references
clinicalPearls: The most common monogenic autoinflammatory disorder, seen predominantly in populations around the Mediterranean basin (Sephardic Jews, Armenians, Turks, Arabs)
Caused by variants in the MEFV gene encoding pyrin, usually inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, leading to dysregulated inflammasome activity
Attacks are self-limited, lasting roughly one to three days, and consist of fever with serositis involving the peritoneum, pleura, or synovium
Abdominal pain from sterile peritonitis is the most frequent feature and can mimic a surgical acute abdomen, sometimes leading to unnecessary laparotomy
An erysipelas-like erythematous rash over the lower leg or ankle is a characteristic though less common finding
Serum acute-phase reactants rise sharply during attacks and often remain mildly elevated between episodes, reflecting subclinical inflammation
Colchicine is the mainstay of long-term therapy and markedly reduces both attack frequency and the risk of secondary amyloidosis; IL-1 inhibitors are used in colchicine-resistant disease
Genetic testing for MEFV supports the diagnosis but is not always definitive, since the diagnosis remains largely clinical and some patients carry only a single identifiable variant
reference.pathophysiology: Loss of normal regulation of the pyrin inflammasome, due to gain-of-function MEFV mutations affecting the pyrin protein, results in inappropriate activation of caspase-1 and excessive release of interleukin-1 beta. This drives recurrent bursts of neutrophil-rich sterile inflammation at serosal and synovial surfaces. Persistent low-grade inflammation between overt attacks promotes deposition of serum amyloid A protein as AA amyloid, the most serious long-term consequence.
additionalDifferentials: Other hereditary periodic fever syndromes (TRAPS, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes, hyper-IgD/mevalonate kinase deficiency)
Acute surgical abdomen (appendicitis, perforated viscus, cholecystitis)
Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis or adult-onset Still disease
additionalInvestigations: Acute-phase reactants (CRP, ESR, serum amyloid A) during and between attacks
MEFV genetic testing to support the clinical diagnosis
Full blood count showing neutrophil leukocytosis during attacks
Urinalysis for proteinuria as an early marker of renal AA amyloidosis
Exclusion of infection and surgical pathology during acute abdominal episodes
redFlags: Persistent proteinuria or nephrotic-range protein loss suggesting secondary AA amyloidosis, which can progress to renal failure
Poor adherence to or resistance against colchicine, raising the cumulative amyloidosis risk
Severe unremitting abdominal pain requiring exclusion of true surgical emergency
Family history of relatives with unexplained renal failure indicating an amyloidosis-prone kindred
reference.prognosis: With regular colchicine prophylaxis most patients have far fewer attacks and a normal life expectancy, and the risk of AA amyloidosis is greatly reduced; untreated or poorly controlled disease carries a significant risk of amyloid nephropathy and end-stage renal disease.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent abdominal pain to a psychosomatic cause and delaying diagnosis for years
Assuming a negative or single-variant MEFV result excludes the disease, since diagnosis is clinical
Stopping colchicine during attack-free periods and losing amyloidosis protection
Overlooking early proteinuria as the first sign of amyloid deposition
